lesson.title: Intermodulation Distortion: When Two Tones Make Unwanted Company
lesson.summary: Intermodulation distortion occurs when a nonlinear circuit is fed two or more frequencies at once and generates new, unwanted tones at their sums and differences, rather than only at integer multiples of each individual tone.
lesson.body:
The harmonic distortion chapter used a single input tone throughout, and the circuit's nonlinearity only ever added multiples of that one frequency. Real audio signals, whether music or voice, are never single tones. They are combinations of many frequencies happening at once, exactly the kind of audio signal you have already studied, made up of components at many different frequencies. When a nonlinear circuit processes several frequencies together, something new happens beyond simple harmonic distortion of each one individually: the nonlinearity also generates entirely new frequencies at the sums and differences of the inputs, along with combinations like twice one frequency minus the other. These new, unwanted tones are intermodulation products, and the overall effect is intermodulation distortion, or IMD.

Here is a worked example on frequencies alone. Suppose two tones, at 1000 Hz and 1200 Hz, are fed simultaneously into a nonlinear stage. The difference frequency is 1200 minus 1000, which is 200 Hz. The sum frequency is 1200 plus 1000, which is 2200 Hz. Higher order products also appear: twice the first tone minus the second is 2000 minus 1200, or 800 Hz, and twice the second tone minus the first is 2400 minus 1000, or 1400 Hz. None of these new frequencies, except by coincidence, are musically related overtones of either original tone, unlike the harmonics produced by distorting a single tone, which are at least octave or overtone related to the note actually being played.

Here is a worked numeric example on amplitude. Suppose the same two tones are each present at 1 V amplitude, and the nonlinearity produces a difference frequency product at 0.03 V and a sum frequency product at 0.015 V. Using an RMS sum approach similar to THD, combine those products relative to a 1 V reference tone: sqrt(0.03 squared plus 0.015 squared) divided by 1. Squaring gives 0.0009 and 0.000225, which sum to 0.001125. The square root of 0.001125 is about 0.0335, so this example works out to about 3.35 percent IMD. Real world test methods, such as the SMPTE and CCIF measurement techniques, define specific standardized tone frequencies, spacings, and weighting for this kind of test; the round numbers used here are chosen to make the calculation method clear rather than to reproduce any one specific named standard's exact test tones.

Intermodulation distortion often sounds more objectionable than an equivalent amount of harmonic distortion, precisely because the new frequencies it creates are not harmonically related to the music being played. Rather than blending in the way musical overtones tend to, they can sound dissonant or harsh against the actual notes. The next chapter groups harmonic distortion and intermodulation distortion together as the two general families that make up audio distortion as a whole.
